paper_title: Towards Full Pipeline FP8 Reinforcement Learning for LLMs

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Reinforcement learning (RL) has become a key technique for improving the reasoning and agentic abilities of large language models (LLMs). Although FP8 quantization can accelerate RL training, maintaining stability throughout an FP8 RL pipeline remains challenging. While previous works have focused on resolving train-inference mismatches using correction techniques like TIS, we reveal that full-pipeline FP8 RL still suffers from severe training instability, manifesting as anomalous mid-training entropy surges and garbled outputs. We trace this instability to a previously overlooked cause: compounded FP8 quantization noise distorts the importance ratio, disproportionately pushing negative-advantage tokens outside the trust region and erroneously zeroing out their gradients. As a result, pathological outputs are not properly penalized and accumulate over the course of training. To address this, we propose Calibrated Clipping, a dynamic method that aligns the FP8 clipping bounds with high-precision BF16 distributions by matching the lower-bound clipping quantile and rebalancing the upper bound accordingly. Extensive experiments across GRPO and DAPO algorithms, model scales from 8B to 32B, and multiple FP8 scaling granularities demonstrate that our approach successfully eliminates entropy surges and restores performance comparable to the BF16 baseline.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content: The success of models such as DeepSeek-R1 [7] and o1 [10] has demonstrated that reinforcement learning (RL) is capable of unlocking long-horizon reasoning and agentic capabilities in LLMs. As RL training continues to scale, improving its efficiency has become increasingly important. Recent advances in low-precision training, especially FP8, provide promising direction for improving efficiency. While FP8 has already been successfully adopted in LLM pretraining [16] and inference [21], recent efforts have begun extending it to RL pipelines. However, enabling stable FP8 RL training remains challenging. Prior work [17, 18] has mainly focused on the mismatch between rollout and training introduced by FP8 quantization. Correction techniques such as truncated importance sampling (TIS, [30]) have been proposed to mitigate this discrepancy, and more recent works [27, 28] have explored unified FP8 pipelinesperforming both rollout and training in FP8to further reduce the precision gap and support on-policy training. Yet we find that training with an FP8 backend suffers from severe instability, manifesting as abrupt mid-training entropy surges (Figure 1) that destabilize training and substantially degrade model performance. 1 Through empirical analysis and controlled case studies, we trace this instability to previously overlooked cause: compounded quantization noise that perturbs the clipping mechanism in PPO-style surrogate objectives. Although the error on individual probabilities remains small, it is amplified in the importance ratio, distorting the effective trust region in quantized space. This effect is especially pronounced at the lower clipping bound, where negative-advantage tokens are disproportionately over-clipped, causing gradients that should suppress pathological generations to vanish prematurely. As result, such pathological outputs are not properly penalized and accumulate over the course of training. To address this, we propose Calibrated Clipping, simple yet effective method for stable FP8 RL training. Our method periodically aligns the lower clipping bound using high-precision BF16 references and adjusts the upper bound to rebalance the contributions of positive and negative updates, restoring the intended trust-region semantics in quantized space with negligible overhead. Our main contributions are as follows: We identify previously overlooked failure mode in full-pipeline FP8 RL: compounded quantization noise in the importance ratio causes systematic over-clipping of tokens, triggering catastrophic mid-training entropy surges. We propose Calibrated Clipping, method that restores trust-region semantics in quantized space by aligning the clipping bounds with high-precision reference. Extensive experiments across GRPO and DAPO algorithms, model sizes from 8B to 32B, and multiple FP8 scaling granularities demonstrate that Calibrated Clipping consistently eliminates entropy surges, restores BF16-level performance, and can achieve up to 1.5 the BF16 training throughput.

sections.title: 2.2 FP8 Quantization
sections.content: The low-precision FP8 format accelerates training and inference but has limited representable range and precision. Thus, tensors are scaled before quantization [6]. Let Fmax denote the largest finite value representable in the chosen FP8 format, and let QFP8 denote rounding and clamping to the FP8 representable set. For high-precision tensor X, the scaled FP8 tensor ˆX and its dequantized approximation (cid:101)X are defined as SX = max(X) Fmax , ˆX = QFP8 (cid:18) SX (cid:19) , (cid:101)X = SX ˆX. (3) The granularity at which the maximum value max(X) is computed dictates the scaling strategy. There are three mainstream scaling strategies: (1) tensorwise scaling, where single scaling factor SX is computed for the entire tensor X; (2) rowwise scaling, where independent scaling factors are calculated for each row of the tensor; and (3) blockwise scaling, where the tensor is partitioned into sub-blocks (e.g., 128 128 elements), with an independent SX assigned to each block [16]. These strategies span spectrum of trade-offs between efficiency and numerical accuracy. Tensorwise scaling maximizes computational efficiency, but its coarse-grained scaling factor is vulnerable to outliers. Blockwise scaling offers the finest-grained adaptation and typically achieves the best numerical fidelity, but at the cost of additional scaling metadata and higher kernel complexity. In practice, FP8 quantization has been widely adopted in LLM inference and pretraining. For example, DeepSeek-V3 [16] was pretrained in FP8 using blockwise scaling. Prior studies [21, 28] have also shown that FP8 inference can improve throughput by around 30% without degrading downstream performance.

sections.title: 2.3 Current Progress in FP8 RL for LLMs
sections.content: Following FP8s successful adoption in LLM pretraining and inference, migrating it to the RL stage is natural progression. However, integrating FP8 into RL introduces unique challenges. Modern RL pipelines consist of two main components: rollout and training. They are usually decoupled in RL frameworks for better performance. Trajectories are sampled by high-throughput inference engines like vLLM [12] and SGLang [36], while updates are computed in training backends like FSDP [33] and Megatron-LM [25]. Previous works [18, 21] have explored adopting FP8 in the rollout stage to accelerate generation. However, ) this design introduces severe trainrollout mismatch: the behavior policy used by the sampler (πFP8 sampler deviates from the learners old policy (πold), even when both are instantiated from the same underlying model parameters. This discrepancy violates the on-policy assumption and can substantially degrade the stability of RL training. To mitigate this issue, truncated importance sampling (TIS, [18, 30]) provides truncated token-level correction: JTIS(θ) = xD, yπFP8 sampler(x) (cid:34) (cid:88) (cid:32) min t=1 (cid:124) πold(yt ht) πFP8 sampler(yt ht) (cid:123)(cid:122) wTIS , (cid:33) (cid:125) min (rt(θ)At, clip (rt(θ), 1 ϵ, 1 + ϵ) At) (cid:35) . Moving beyond using FP8 for rollout alone, more recent works [27, 28] have explored unified FP8 pipeline in which both rollout and training are performed in FP8. These studies showed that, compared with mixedprecision designs such as BF16 training with FP8 rollout, unified FP8 pipeline can narrow the trainrollout log-probability gap, thereby improving overall training stability. However, as we show in the following sections, there are additional sources of instability that must be explicitly addressed to enable robust, full-pipeline FP8 RL training. 3 Figure 1 Comparison of (left) actor entropy, (middle) average evaluation accuracy on downstream tasks, and (right) PPO clipping fraction during the training of Qwen3-8B-Base under different settings.

sections.title: 3 Case Study
sections.content: To investigate the stability of full-pipeline FP8 RL, we train Qwen3-8B-Base on the DeepScaleR dataset [26] using GRPO with 16K context length. We compare the standard BF16 baseline against configurations using FP8 rollout paired with four training backends: (1) BF16, (2) tensorwise FP8, (3) rowwise FP8, and (4) blockwise FP8. We adopt TIS by default in all experiments. The Phenomenon: Anomalous Entropy Surges. As shown in Figure 1, we monitor the response entropy as an indicator of training stability. While the BF16 and FP8-Rollout-BF16-Train settings remain stable, the models trained with FP8 backends experience anomalous surges in entropy in the middle of training, typically after 100 steps. Consistent with our previous analysis, finer-grained scaling strategies mitigate quantization noise and lead to relatively milder surges; however, even with blockwise scaling, this pathological instability persists, resulting in substantial performance disparity compared to the BF16 baseline. Since this instability persists across all scaling granularities, we adopt rowwise FP8 as the representative configuration to diagnose the underlying mechanics. As illustrated in Figure 2, we analyze the composition of response entropies by partitioning them into four discrete bins: [0, 0.2), [0.2, 0.5), [0.5, 1.0), and [1.0, ). Our analysis reveals that the global entropy surge is non-uniform; while the vast majority of responses maintain healthy entropy levels (< 0.5), the surge is driven by small but rapidly proliferating fraction of samples exhibiting pathological entropy (> 1.0), which spikes sharply in frequency after 100 steps. After inspecting these high-entropy responses, we find that they generally contain large proportion of garbled, fragmented, or nonsensical tokens, signifying collapse in the models decoding state (Figure 8). Further analysis of the associated advantages shows that only 6.64% of them yield positive advantages. With the policy optimization described in Section 2.1, the remaining majority should be penalized to suppress their occurrence. Yet we observe that their prevalence continues to grow. The Cause: Compounded Noise and Over-Clipping. We trace this counterintuitive failure to the interaction between FP8 quantization noise and the PPO clipping mechanism. In full-pipeline FP8 training, the probabilities for both πθ and πold are induced by FP8-quantized forward passes. Using BF16 shadow passes for diagnosis, we measured the normalized mean absolute error (NMAE) of these FP8-induced probabilities relative to high-precision references. As illustrated in Figure 3, while the quantization error for individual probabilities is marginal, the ratio operation significantly compounds this noise, enlarging the discrepancy by 1.7 to 2.9. This compounded noise inflates the frequency at which tokens hit the trust region boundaries, phenomenon 1 ϵ; we define as over-clipping. token is lower-bound over-clipped if At < 0, rBF16 > 1 ϵ, and rFP8 analogously, it is upper-bound over-clipped if At > 0, rBF16 1 + ϵ. The PPO clipping fractions shown in Figure 1 provide empirical evidence for this phenomenon. Even with fine-grained blockwise scaling, the PPO clipping fraction remains nearly 4 higher than in the BF16 baseline. < 1 + ϵ, and rFP8 Our evaluation of these over-clipped tokens reveals two asymmetric trends (Figure 4): 4 Figure 2 Composition of entropy across training steps in rowwise FP8 training. Figure 3 Normalized MAE of probabilities and importance ratios from the FP8 model relative to BF16 references. During the later stages of training, approximately 70% of over-clipping occurs at the lower bound (1 ϵ). Nearly 90% of these lower-bound over-clipped tokens originate from the high-entropy responses identified in Figure 2. Figure 4 Analysis of over-clipping: (Left) Proportion of over-clipping occurrences at the lower bound (1 ϵ). (Right) Proportion of lower-bound over-clipped tokens originating from high-entropy responses. We identify the failure loop as follows: when the model generates garbled responses with negative advantages, the policy optimization attempts to penalize them. However, the compounded FP8 noise frequently pushes the importance ratios below the 1 ϵ threshold, falsely triggering the clipping mechanism and zeroing out the gradients. This premature gradient vanishing prevents the model from unlearning pathological behaviors, allowing garbled outputs to proliferate and eventually destabilize training. Empirical Verification and Implications. To verify our analysis, we reran the rowwise FP8 experiment, relaxing the lower clipping bound from 0.8 to 0.6. As shown in Figure 5, this simple adjustment successfully prevented the catastrophic mid-training entropy surge. 5 Figure 5 Relaxing the lower bound in rowwise FP8 training prevents the entropy surge (left) but leads to premature entropy saturation, lower training rewards (middle), and shorter responses (right). However, it introduces new problem. While looser lower bound restores the ability to penalize garbled responses, it results in excessive negative updates that cause the entropy to saturate prematurely. This over-penalization also hurts model performance; as shown in Figure 5, the average reward and response length remain consistently lower than the BF16 baseline, suggesting that the model has become overly conservative. These results demonstrate that relaxing the lower bound in isolation is insufficient. We need principled approach to rebalance the trust region.

sections.title: 4 Solution: Calibrated Clipping
sections.content: Integrating FP8 into the training backend alters the trust region landscape. Under the FP8 regime, probabilities = Q(rt; θ, θold), where Q() are computed via quantized forward passes, yielding the importance ratio: rFP8 captures the compounded, nonlinear effect of FP8 quantization. To preserve the original trust region semantics, the ideal clipping bounds [L, H] should satisfy = Q(1 ϵ; θ, θold), = Q(1 + ϵ; θ, θold). In practice, the exact formulation of Q() is intractable. As discussed in Section 3, the lower boundary is particularly important: garbled responses predominantly carry negative advantages, and FP8-induced ratio perturbations increase the likelihood that their ratios cross this boundary. Thus, we propose Calibrated Clipping, method that dynamically reconstructs the trust region through two stages: 1. Lower-Bound Alignment. We first align the clipping quantile of the FP8 distribution with that of BF16 for negative-advantage tokens. The goal is to ensure that the proportion of negative-advantage tokens clipped at the lower bound in the FP8 domain matches that in BF16. For given training step, let FBF16,(r) and FFP8,(r) denote the cumulative distribution functions (CDFs) of the importance ratios under BF16 and FP8, respectively, restricted to tokens with At < 0. We first determine the target clipping quantile αlow from the reference BF16 distribution: αlow = FBF16,(1 ϵ). We then derive the calibrated lower bound by applying the inverse CDF to the FP8 distribution: = 1 FP8,(αlow). Replacing 1 ϵ with the calibrated quantile equalizes the number of lower-clipped tokens under the two precisions and effectively prevents over-clipping. 2. Upper-Bound Rebalancing. To mitigate over-penalization from relaxed lower bound, we rebalance the positive-to-negative update ratio. In Section 2.1, we showed that the effective contribution to the surrogate objective can be decomposed into positive and negative parts. Both stages of our method require BF16 reference results. At each recalibration step, we perform two forward-only BF16 shadow passes over the same training batch, evaluating the current policy πBF16 using their master weights. We then compute the reference importance and the old policy πBF16 ratios rBF16 . However, performing these additional forward passes at every training step would negate the performance gains of FP8 training. old θ Fortunately, we find that the calibrated trust region does not fluctuate drastically when training is stable. Figure 6 illustrates the trajectory of the calibrated lower bound derived from our case study in Section 3. Mirroring the evolution of actor entropy, the calibrated bound remains stable after the initial phase of training. Notable inter-step deviations are only observed in the later stages during entropy surges. Leveraging this stability, we can amortize the overhead by periodically recalculating the clipping bounds rather than performing per-step alignment. Our method is formalized in Algorithm 1. We define the search intervals as IL = [0.5, 0.9] for the lower bound and IH = [1.2, 2.0] for the upper bound, employing search step size of = 0.02. We define SmoothUpdate(b, b, δ) = + clip ((b b)/2, δ, δ), with maximum update magnitudes δL = 0.05 and δH = 0.1. This prevents abrupt shifts in the trust region, maintaining smooth evolution. We initialize the clipping bounds at [0.6, 1.8] for faster convergence and perform updates every 20 training steps. While these hyperparameters were not explicitly tuned, they demonstrate robust performance across all evaluated settings. We evaluate the sensitivity to the update interval and clipping-bound initialization in Appendix A.5.

sections.title: 5 Evaluation
sections.content: All experiments use VeRL [24] as the RL framework, vLLM [12] as the inference engine, and TorchAO [19] 7 as the FP8 training engine. We integrate the patch provided by FlashRL [18] for FP8 rollout. To compare training stability across settings, all reported metrics were collected over the final 50% of training steps. Experiment configurations and additional training metricssuch as actor entropy, rewards, response lengths, clipping fractions, and calibrated clipping boundsare detailed in the Appendix.

sections.content: We train Qwen3-8B-Base and Qwen2.5-32B with GRPO on the DeepScaleR dataset [26]. We evaluate the models on eight widely used reasoning benchmarks, including AIME24/25 [1], OlympiadBench [8], Gaokao [32], MATH-500 [9, 15], Minerva Math [13], and AMC23/24 [2]. sections.title: 5.3 Performance Gains
sections.content: We focus on performance gains within the training phase enabled by full-pipeline FP8 training, benchmarking across 8B, 14B, and 32B models at sequence lengths of 4K, 8K, and 16K. As shown in Figure 7, coarser scaling granularities generally yield greater throughput improvements. Tensorwise scaling typically achieves up to 1.5 the BF16 training throughput, while blockwise scaling can also provide 10%20% improvement. 9 These training gains, together with the approximately 30% generation speedup from FP8 rollout reported by prior work [18], enable substantial full-pipeline efficiency improvements.

sections.title: 6 Related Work & Discussion
sections.content: Related RL Algorithms and Clipping Mechanisms. Several works have sought to improve RL stability by redesigning the clipping mechanism. DAPO [31] proposes asymmetrically relaxing the upper bound to encourage exploration. GSPO [34] reconceives the trust region at the sequence level, applying clipping over entire responses rather than individual tokens. Beyond importance-ratio clipping, M2PO [35] identifies extreme updates using batch-level second-moment statistic over log-importance ratios, while DPPO [20] directly determines the trust region from policy divergence. Our analysis focuses on token-level clipping in GRPO and DAPO. Sequence-level aggregation may reduce sensitivity to individual token-ratio errors, but precision-induced distortion may still affect the aggregated sequence ratio; extending calibration to sequence-level clipping remains future work. Chen et al. [4] connect clipping bias to policy-entropy reduction under spurious rewards, while Karaman et al. [11] decouple importance-weight clipping for correct and incorrect responses to balance exploration and training stability. These studies analyze entropy control under reward or off-policy effects; our work instead focuses on false lower-bound clipping induced by FP8 ratio distortion. CISPO [3] is closely related to our work. It addresses gradient zeroing from hard clipping by retaining gradient contributions from clipped tokens and clipping only the sampling weights. However, CISPO was not designed for FP8 RL. As shown in Appendix A.2, applying CISPO to rowwise FP8 training leads to training collapse after 300 steps, indicating that the clipping boundaries still need to be carefully calibrated. BAPO [29] proposes dynamically adjusting the clipping bounds to rebalance positive and negative contributions. While BAPO adjusts its bounds to satisfy predefined threshold on the positive contribution to the policy loss, our Calibrated Clipping derives the lower bound and the target ratio directly from high-precision reference and solves for the upper bound accordingly. In similar rowwise-FP8 experiment, BAPO becomes unstable after approximately 90 steps and eventually collapses as its clipping bounds move to [0.9, 3.0]; detailed trajectories are provided in Appendix A.3. This result indicates that fixed contribution target does not stabilize this FP8 setting. FP8 RL for LLMs. Early efforts on FP8 RL focus exclusively on the rollout stage. FlashRL [18] demonstrates that FP8 generation yields an approximately 30% speedup but introduces traininference mismatch. Efforts to mitigate this mismatch primarily focus on correcting it via importance sampling. Truncated Importance Sampling (TIS, [30]) and Masked Importance Sampling (MIS, [17]) provide corrections at the token and sequence levels, respectively. QuRL [14] further refines TIS by incorporating the proximal-to-behavior policy ratio into the clipping range. More recent works, including Jet-RL [28] and Unified FP8 [27], extend FP8 to both rollout and training, showing that full-pipeline unification narrows the trainrollout precision gap and facilitates on-policy training. These works share our motivation but focus on the precision gap; none identifies the failure mode we characterize: compounded quantization noise in the importance ratio systematically distorts the clipping mechanism, causing over-clipping and ultimately destabilizing training.

sections.title: 7 Conclusion
sections.content: We investigate the stability of full-pipeline FP8 RL for LLMs and identify previously overlooked failure mode: compounded FP8 quantization noise distorts the importance ratio, causing systematic over-clipping that triggers pathological entropy surges. To address this, we propose Calibrated Clipping, which dynamically realigns the clipping bounds by matching the FP8 clipping quantile to high-precision BF16 reference and rebalancing the positive-to-negative update ratio. Extensive experiments demonstrate that Calibrated Clipping consistently eliminates entropy surges and restores BF16-level performance while achieving up to 1.5 the BF16 training throughput, establishing practical path toward full-pipeline FP8 RL for LLMs.

sections.content: A.1 Example of High-Entropy Response Figure 8 An example of high-entropy response containing garbled and fragmented tokens. A.2 Results of the CISPO Experiment We train Qwen3-8B-Base on the DeepScaleR dataset using CISPO, with all remaining configurations identical to those of the GRPO experiments in Section 5.1. As shown in Figure 9, training collapses after approximately 300 steps, with entropy spiking sharply and reward dropping to zero. This demonstrates that retaining clipped gradients is insufficient to stabilize training in this rowwise-FP8 setting. Figure 9 Training entropy and reward of rowwise FP8 CISPO training. A.3 Results of the BAPO Experiment We evaluate BAPO in the same Qwen3-8B GRPO setting as Section 5.1, using rowwise FP8 training and FP8 rollout. We use the default BAPO configuration [29]: target positive-token contribution ρ0 = 0.4, lower-bound range [0.6, 0.9], upper-bound range [1.2, 3.0], and update steps δlow = 0.02 and δhigh = 0.05. As shown in Figure 10, the positive-token contribution ρ falls below its target after approximately 90 steps, while BAPO progressively moves the lower and upper clipping bounds toward 0.9 and 3.0, respectively. Training subsequently becomes unstable, and the reward eventually collapses to zero. In this FP8 setting, using fixed positive-contribution target therefore fails to stabilize training. A.4 Results on the Eurus Dataset We further evaluate Calibrated Clipping by training Qwen3-8B on the coding subset of Eurus-2-RL-Data [5] and evaluating on TACO, APPS, and Codeforces. As shown in Table 3, Calibrated Clipping improves the average score over vanilla FP8 training for all three scaling granularities. 13 Figure 10 BAPO with rowwise FP8 training in the Qwen3-8B GRPO setting. From left to right: actor entropy, reward, positive-token contribution ρ, upper clipping bound, and lower clipping bound.

A.5 Sensitivity to Calibration Hyperparameters We evaluate the sensitivity of our method to two hyperparameters in the same Qwen3-8B rowwise-FP8 GRPO setting as Section 3: the recalibration interval and the initialization of the clipping bounds. For the recalibration interval, we compare updates every 10, 20, and 40 training steps. For the initialization, we compare the default bounds [0.6, 1.8] with the standard bounds [0.8, 1.2]. As shown in Table 4, changing the recalibration interval or the initial clipping bounds affects the final average score to some extent, but every tested configuration recovers substantial performance over vanilla rowwise FP8 training, demonstrating the robustness of our method.
